summary: A belated report on a network meeting, written by Vint Cerf in 1970. It records what was discussed rather than defining a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A late write-up of what happened at a meeting.

subtitle: A meeting report from the early network working group

tldr.problem: The network working group needed to document what was discussed at a May 1970 meeting at Lincoln Labs about message formats and record structures for host-to-host communication.
tldr.mechanism: Vint Cerf wrote a brief report recording the decisions made: records can begin anywhere in a message, the first 8 bits mark the record type, and several standard types were agreed on for different data formats.
tldr.outcome: This early standardization on type bytes helped establish conventions for network messages during the ARPANET's infancy.

today: RFC 63 is an informational document and has not been obsoleted. It remains a historical record of early ARPANET protocol decisions.

sections.title: A Meeting Report from Lincoln Labs
sections.content:
RFC 63 records what was discussed at a Network Working Group meeting held on 8 May 1970 at Lincoln Labs. Vint Cerf wrote the report, listing three main topics: the Local Interaction Language, messages and record formats for host-to-host exchange, and miscellaneous issues.

The most significant discussion involved RFC 42's proposal that all messages start with an 8-bit type byte to declare the message format. The group made concrete decisions about how records should be structured within network messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Scientists met to talk about how to send messages between computers. They decided that each message needs a label at the start saying what kind of message it is.

sections.title: Type Bytes and Message Structure
sections.content:
The group agreed that records could begin anywhere within a message, and that the first 8 bits of a record are reserved for type information. The first transmission on a connection starts a record.

Type 0 means an arbitrarily long bit string follows with no further type bytes. Types 1 through 3 specify different character encodings: 8-bit ASCII, EBCDIC, and MOD 33 TTY 7-bit ASCII. Types 4 and 5 allow local format extensions, each followed by another type byte.
sections.plainLanguage: They agreed on simple labels: type 0 means raw data, type 1 means regular text, types 2 and 3 mean different computer text codes, and types 4 and 5 are for special local formats.

sections.title: Document Status and Attribution
sections.content:
The report credits all attendees, including researchers from Lincoln Labs, Harvard, UCLA, UTAH, MITRE, RAND, SDC, SRI, and Raytheon. Notably, the document also records that Jim Torson would take over receiving RFC submissions from Chuck Rose at Case University.

This document is an early example of how the network working group documented consensus decisions and provides historical context for early ARPANET protocol development.
sections.plainLanguage: The note lists all the scientists who were at the meeting and says who would handle paperwork for future notes.
